The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven to the coast for a weekend getaway, and I remember standing on the warm sand, staring at the endless blue horizon. The waves crashed against the shore, and I felt something inside me shift—like a tiny door had opened to something vast and unknown. I didn’t understand it then, but that moment planted a seed. Years later, I’d realize it was wonder, that gnawing, beautiful ache for the unknown.

Now, I chase that feeling. Not just in oceans, but in books, in late-night drives with the windows down, in the quiet hum of a library, in the way rain sounds on a tin roof. Wonder isn’t just in grand landscapes; it’s in the way light filters through leaves or how a stranger’s laugh can feel like a secret just for you. It’s in the pause before you turn a page, in the breath you take when you see something so beautiful it hurts.

But wonder is fragile. It thrives in curiosity, wilts under cynicism. The older I get, the harder it is to hold onto—to-do lists and deadlines and the weight of responsibilities can dull its edges. That’s why I try to cultivate it, like a garden. I take walks without a destination. I listen to music that makes my chest tighten. I let myself be surprised.

Because wonder is the antidote to the ordinary. It’s the reason we keep looking up, keep reaching, keep hoping. Even when the world feels heavy, even when the horizon is obscured by clouds, wonder reminds us that there’s always more—more to see, more to feel, more to be. And that’s enough.
